This bill is part of a package that creates a legislative framework for national automated identity matching services used by government and industry.

The package would authorise one-to-one identity checks with consent through the Document Verification Service and Face Verification Service, and one-to-many matching only to protect legally assumed identities.
Around 2.6 million Face Verification Service transactions occurred in the 2022-23 financial year, and the bill would impose privacy safeguards including consent, breach reporting and annual audits.
Authorises public and private entities to use one-to-one identity matching services with the individual's consent.
Prohibits one-to-many facial matching except to protect legally assumed identities such as undercover officers.
Allows the Attorney-General's Department to develop and operate the identity verification facilities.
Creates offences for unauthorised recording, disclosure or access of protected information by entrusted persons.
Requires state and territory authorities to inform individuals if their data is stored on the National Driver Licence Facial Recognition Solution.
Establishes annual compliance reporting and assessments by the Information Commissioner.
Government agencies, private sector entities including banks, and individuals whose identity is verified through the services.

This bill would amend the Water Act 2007 and the Basin Plan to fully implement the Murray-Darling Basin Plan and reform water markets.

It would remove the 1,500 gigalitre cap on Commonwealth water purchases, allow flexible use of Water for the Environment Special Account funds, and extend deadlines for Basin States to deliver projects.
The bill sets a 31 December 2027 deadline for final contracts to recover 450 gigalitres of additional environmental water, with a reconciliation by 31 December 2026.
Removes the statutory 1,500 gigalitre limit on Commonwealth water purchases.
Allows the Water for the Environment Special Account funds to be used for water purchase programs for the 450 gigalitre target.
Extends the deadline for Basin States to deliver Sustainable Diversion Limit Adjustment Mechanism projects to December 2026.
Gives the Inspector-General of Water Compliance power to determine if a Basin State has a reasonable excuse for exceeding a Sustainable Diversion Limit by 20% or more.
Delays the Water Act review until 2027.
Requires Basin States to provide action plans and progress reports to the Inspector-General for any Sustainable Diversion Limit exceedances.

Basin communities, agriculture, industry, First Nations, irrigation, tourism, recreation, cultural users, drinking water consumers, the Murray-Darling Basin Authority, the Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder, Basin States, and water market participants in the Murray-Darling Basin.

This bill updates Australian law to align with international rules that allow carbon dioxide to be sent overseas for storage under the seabed and permit certain ocean-based climate experiments.

It would create two new permit types: one for exporting captured carbon dioxide for burial in geological formations beneath the sea floor, and another for placing materials in the ocean for marine geoengineering research.
The bill also makes small adjustments to existing rules and updates the language of the law, without adding any new fees or changing who enforces the rules.
Introduces permits for exporting carbon dioxide streams for sub-seabed storage.
Introduces permits for placing wastes or other matter for marine geoengineering research.
Makes consequential amendments to support the new permits.
Makes technical updates to simplify the law's wording.
Companies and researchers involved in carbon capture, export, and marine geoengineering, as well as the agency that issues sea dumping permits.

This bill changes the Migration Act 1958 to make document delivery rules clearer and to let more people apply for protection visas.
It would require written notices for all visa cancellations, allow regulations to set delivery methods, and treat documents as valid if the person actually gets them despite minor errors.
The bill would also remove the ban that stops people with multiple nationalities or certain residency rights from lodging protection visa applications.
All cancellation-related notices must be in writing.
The minister can give documents by any method if the person receives them, even if there are minor errors.
A document is considered compliant if the minister mostly followed the rules and the person's rights are not seriously harmed.
The bill removes the legal barrier that prevented some non-citizens from applying for protection visas.
People applying for protection visas, the Minister, the Department, and the Administrative Appeals Tribunal and courts.

The bill would expand the office that oversees live animal exports to give it a stronger animal welfare role.
It would rename the office to include animal welfare in its title and add new powers to review administrative systems and reporting.
The new office would be independent and could not be directed by anyone except as the Act allows, and would follow a written ministerial direction for a specific review.
Expands the office's focus to animal welfare and renames it.
Adds objects to monitor and report on animal welfare and export laws.
Allows the office to review Commonwealth administrative systems and reporting.
Makes the office independent with complete discretion in its work.
Requires the office to conduct a review if the Minister directs it in writing.
Allows the office to conduct a review if requested by certain other ministers or the Agriculture Department Secretary.
The office of the Inspector-General, the Minister, the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, and livestock export stakeholders.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2023-05-31.136.1) to agree with the main idea of the bill. According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2223a/23bd087): * *The Bill renames the Inspector-General of Live Animal Exports Act 2019 as the Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Exports Act 2019. The title of the Inspector-General is similarly renamed.* * *The Inspector-General’s functions are expanded to include the conduct of reviews of, amongst other things, the performance of functions, or exercise of powers by livestock export officials under live animal export legislation and standards. The objects of the Inspector-General of Animal Welfare and Live Exports Act are amended to reflect the new functions.* * *The Bill expressly states that the Inspector-General is independent and has complete discretion in the performance of their functions and the exercise of their powers.* * *In acknowledgement of the expanded functions, the Bill provides for officers and employees of the Commonwealth public service to assist the Inspector-General and for consultants to be engaged.* * *The Bill requires the Inspector-General to prepare and publish an annual work plan for each financial year.* * *Animal protection organisations have raised concerns in relation to the scope of the Inspector-General’s functions and have called for the expansion of the role to include oversight of animal welfare standards in all Commonwealth-regulated fields. Industry bodies support the Bill’s restriction of oversight to animal welfare in the context of live export.*

The bill would change the main family law Act to make separation less complicated and focus on what is best for children.
It would rewrite the part of the Act that deals with parenting orders, add rules for hearing children's views, and give courts a new power to stop repeated legal harassment.
The changes would also bring forward a review of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Act by two years.
Simplify the framework for deciding parenting arrangements and children's best interests.
Allow children to express their views to an Independent Children's Lawyer in appropriate cases.
Create a new court power to prevent systems abuse by stopping repetitive applications.
Better recognise Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children's cultural rights and kinship concepts.
Make the consequences of not following parenting orders clearer.
Introduce harmful proceedings orders to stop vexatious litigants filing without court permission.
Separating families, children, family courts, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

This means that the bill will now return to the House of Representatives, where our MPs will decide on whether they agree with the [Senate amendments](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fsched%2Fr7011_sched_20d5e2f4-d8ff-4ed8-a047-5285cbbe7b1d%22;rec=0) and so allow the bills to become law. ### What does the bill do? The Family Law Amendment (Information Sharing) Bill 2023 was moved to enhance information sharing between family law courts and state/territory child protection, police and firearms authorities, introducing new court orders for particulars and production of documents, and safeguards for sensitive information, with the aim of improving child safety and closing gaps between federal and state systems.

The Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2023, the Infrastructure Australia Amendment (Independent Review) Bill 2023, the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023, the Family Law Amendment (Information Sharing) Bill 2023, and the Crimes and Other Legislation Amendment (Omnibus) Bill 2023 were referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration at the adjournment of the debate on the second reading of each bill.

The coalition member argued the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023 contains untested solutions that could worsen outcomes for Australian families, opposing the repeal of the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility and raising concerns about enforcement, Indigenous children provisions, and independent children's lawyers.

The coalition supports the intent of many measures in the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023 but cannot support it without further scrutiny, citing concerns over practical impacts in remote areas, lack of consultation on a review date change for the Federal Circuit and Family Court merger, and inadequate testing of solutions. The coalition will back a committee inquiry to examine the bill before finalising its position.

The member moved amendments to the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023 requiring a reasonable attempt to consult on long‑term decisions, codifying the *Rice v Asplund* test for reopening final parenting orders before any hearing, and requiring a reasonable attempt to understand obligations as a defence to contravention. Further amendments sought to include family violence history and family violence orders as mandatory considerations, define repeated legal systems abuse as family violence, and add cultural‑linguistic background factors for children’s best interests. The government did not support the amendments, noting the bill would be referred to a committee.
Fair Work Amendment (Paid Family and Domestic Violence Leave) Bill 2022

The member argued that the Fair Work Amendment (Paid Family and Domestic Violence Leave) Bill 2022 is a crucial reform after a 10-year campaign but stressed that addressing root causes such as gender inequality and outdated stereotypes, along with prevention and perpetrator programs, is also necessary.

The speaker argued that skills shortages in Australia result from a decade of poor workforce planning under the previous government, not just the pandemic, and announced the Jobs and Skills Australia Bill 2022 would establish a new agency to address this. Concrete commitments include 180,000 fee-free TAFE places in 2023, $100 million for 10,000 new energy apprenticeships, and a target of 70% of Commonwealth VET funding for public TAFE.

The speaker defended the Climate Change Bill 2022, arguing it implements Labor’s election policy of a 43% emissions reduction by 2030, 82% renewable energy by 2030, and lower energy prices by 2025, while criticising the member for Fairfax for ignoring facts and accusing the former government of hiding a report on rising energy prices.
Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022

The Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection And Appointment) Bill 2022 is necessary to ensure transparent, merit-based appointments and restore public trust, as the commission itself has long advocated—citing President Rosalind Croucher’s 1 August letter and the December 2021 Free and Equal position paper. The speaker also called for a national bill or charter of human rights to provide a legislative framework for rights and responsibilities.
National Health Amendment (Enhancing the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme) Bill 2021

The speaker criticised the Morrison government for failing to proactively address medicine supply chain disruptions, noting 263 medicines in shortage and citing a constituent unable to access Actemra; they argued for Labor's proposed $15 billion reconstruction fund to support local manufacturing and called for Trikafta to be listed on the PBS for cystic fibrosis patients.
Electoral Legislation Amendment (Counting, Scrutiny and Operational Efficiencies) Bill 2021

The speaker argued for fixed four-year federal terms, a national integrity commission, truth in political advertising, and other structural reforms to restore trust in democracy, noting that over 16,500 First Nations Australians in the Northern Territory cannot vote. He supported the Electoral Legislation Amendment bill but said it does not go far enough.
National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Improving Supports for At Risk Participants) Bill 2021

The speaker argued that the Morrison government's COVID-19 vaccine rollout for people with disability has been a negligent failure, noting that only about 26.9% of NDIS participants aged over 16 and fewer than 50% of those in group homes are fully vaccinated.
